description: Newbies in space research looking to explore and go where no human has gone before.
summary:
Martian Odyssey is a free browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. The player runs a Mars outpost for 16 sols (Mars days). Each sol brings a problem, and the player picks one of about four crew action cards. Every card helps something and costs something: making oxygen uses water and power, and hiding from a solar flare costs a day of science. The player has to keep six meters safe (power, oxygen, water, food, radiation dose and waste) and still earn enough science to win.

This answers the challenge because no choice is free. An automated test fails the build if any card has no cost or is strictly better than another. The game also runs on real NASA data. The solar flares come from DONKI records of the May 2024 solar storm. The daily radiation dose is the real reading from the Curiosity rover. Every source is credited inside the game.

It matters because kids learn real limits of living in space by making the trade-offs themselves, not by reading facts.
details:
Martian Odyssey: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

Source code: https://github.com/srivastavaanika/martian-outpost-game

What does it do and how does it work?

Martian Odyssey is a browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. The player is the captain of a Mars outpost for 16 sols (Mars days), from Sol 215 to Sol 230. To win, they have to keep the crew safe and collect enough science (shown as Coins) by the last sol.

The outpost has six meters, each in real units:

  • Power in kilowatt-hours (kWh)
  • Oxygen in kilograms (kg)
  • Water in kilolitres (kL)
  • Food in kilograms (kg)
  • Radiation dose in millisieverts (mSv)
  • Waste in kilograms (kg)

Each sol works like this:

  1. Something happens. Each sol is tied to a real Earth date in May 2024, during one of the strongest solar storms in 20 years. If NASA's DONKI database lists a large X-class solar flare on that date, the outpost gets a Solar Flare Warning labelled with the real flare class and date (for example "X8.7"). On other sols, one of eight other problems comes up, such as a dust storm, a pipe leak, a crack in the dome or a rover stuck in sand. Smaller real flares that day add a small extra radiation dose.
  2. The player picks one of about four crew action cards. Every card helps something and costs something. For example, Make oxygen from water gives air but uses water and power, and Dash to the storm bunker blocks the radiation but loses a day of science. Any meter in its danger zone always gets a card that can fix it.
  3. The sol plays out. The card's effects apply first, then whatever part of the problem the card didn't prevent, then each meter's daily change. The mission ends early if power, oxygen, water or food hits zero, or if radiation or waste hits its limit.

When the mission ends, a debrief explains what happened in kid-friendly language. It gives the real-world lesson behind each card the player used, plus a real NASA fact.

All the game rules live in one pure TypeScript engine that has no user interface code in it. A React interface and an animated 2D Phaser scene of the outpost only display what the engine decides.

What benefits does it have?

  • It teaches real trade-offs, not just facts. Kids feel that saving power today can cost oxygen tomorrow. The meters are linked the way they are on a real base:
    • Making oxygen uses water and power.
    • Plants drink water and give back a little air.
    • Spacewalks use suit oxygen and add radiation.
    • Recycling water also cuts down waste.
  • It uses real data, and says where it came from. The solar flares are real NASA DONKI records, and the daily Mars radiation dose (0.67 mSv per day) is the real measurement from Curiosity's Radiation Assessment Detector at Gale Crater. A Data Sources screen in the game credits every NASA source and image.
  • It's honest about what's real. Real values are labelled with their source, and game-balance numbers are labelled as game numbers. The built-in flare data is never shown as live; a separate panel labelled LIVE can fetch current flares from DONKI.
  • It's easy to access. It's a free static website with no login and no backend, so it runs on school Chromebooks, tablets and phones (tested down to a 375 px wide screen). It uses big touch targets, colour is never the only signal, and animations respect the device's reduced-motion setting.
  • It's short. One mission fits in a classroom session.

What is the intended impact?

We want a child to finish a mission understanding at least one real limit of living in deep space. For example: you make oxygen from water, solar storms force you to choose between shelter and work, and dust storms cut solar power. They should also leave knowing that the solar storm in the game really happened.

The game is tuned so learning pays off. In 2,000 simulated games per strategy:

Strategy

Win rate

Picking cards at random

28.6%

Following the "Fixes ..." hints on the cards

54.1%

Always grabbing the most science

0.0%

Watching every meter and balancing

99.3%

Thinking carefully about trade-offs nearly always wins. Being greedy with science never does.

Teachers can use it to start conversations about life support, space weather, radiation safety and how NASA plans missions.

What tools, coding languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • Language: TypeScript (strict mode)
  • Frontend: React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, Framer Motion, Zustand for state
  • 2D scene: Phaser 3
    • Vitest unit tests, including a design-rules test that fails the build if any choice is free or strictly better than another.
    • A Playwright end-to-end smoke test.
    • ESLint and Prettier.
    • A headless balance simulator that plays thousands of games per strategy.
  • Development tools: Node.js, Git/GitHub, and Cursor (AI-assisted code editor).
  • Hardware: standard laptops. No special hardware is needed to play; any modern browser works.

How is the project creative?

  • Real space weather becomes the story. The mission runs on the dates of the May 2024 solar storm, so the biggest scares in the game are flares that really happened. When kids see "X8.7", it's a real event.
  • No safe choice exists, and a test enforces it. An automated test checks every card in the game and fails the build if any card is free or strictly better than another.
  • The game helps kids who are struggling. When a meter gets low, the card that can fix it is guaranteed to show up, and it's tagged "Fixes ...". This means younger players learn from mistakes instead of being punished. In a crisis, science cards drop out of the hand, which mirrors how real crews put survival ahead of research.
  • It's honest about images. No Mars outpost exists yet, so we use NASA's artist's concept and label it "not a photo". The welcome screen puts together real NASA photos and says so.
  • It has a debrief, not just a "Game Over". Every ending explains what happened and the real lesson behind it, using gentle language with no scary words about dying.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Age group: The text follows our own content guidelines: short sentences, simple words, friendly tone, and the real terms explained (with a glossary in the repo).
    • Each sol is mapped to one Earth date.
    • The radiation budget is 40 mSv for the mission. NASA's real career limit is 600 mSv, which 16 days could never reach.
  • How many resources to show: The challenge suggests two or three. We chose six on purpose, because the links between oxygen, water, power and food are the lesson. We kept it manageable with clear gauges, danger warnings and guaranteed fix cards. The decision is recorded in the project's decision log.
  • Balance: We retuned with the simulator until careful play wins almost every time and greedy play loses.
  • Accessibility and reach: It's a free static site with no accounts, works on phones and tablets, has large touch targets, doesn't rely on colour alone, and respects reduced-motion settings.
  • Data honesty and credit: Bundled data is never shown as live, every NASA source is credited in the game, and NASA logos aren't used.
  • Keeping the code easy to maintain: The game rules are a pure engine with seeded randomness, so results can be replayed. The user interface and scene only display results, which lets judges and teachers check the rules separately from the visuals.
